Lutjanus malabaricus exhibits a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 20% [GSI = 20%] when water temperatures reach 28 °C [T = 28 °C] during the spawning season. Field collections from the Great Barrier Reef indicate that females attain sexual maturation at a fork length of 57.6 centimeters [Lp = 57.6 centimeters], a size that corresponds to approximately two to three years of age under average regional conditions. This length at puberty is comparable to that reported for related species such as Lutjanus erythropterus, although direct comparative data remain limited. Histological examination of ovarian tissue confirms that all females above this size threshold are reproductively active during the peak of the season, whereas smaller individuals show no evidence of vitellogenic oocyte development.

The pelagic larval phase begins with the release of small, transparent eggs that measure approximately 0.85 millimeters in diameter, comparable to the egg size documented for the congener Lutjanus stellatus. Based on this egg dimension, the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], which is consistent with the initial mass reported for other Lutjanus species with planktotrophic larvae. After hatching, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-eclosion, undergoing rapid organogenesis before the onset of exogenous feeding. The mouth gape opening occurs around day three post-hatching, at which point the larvae begin to consume small copepod nauplii. The transition from yolk dependence to active feeding represents a critical bottleneck for survival, as mortality rates during this period are high in both wild and captive settings. Growth during the larval stage is strongly temperature dependent, with faster development rates observed at warmer water temperatures.

As juveniles transition to the benthic habitat, they seek shelter in nearshore reef environments characterized by abundant structural complexity. The ultimate fork length for this species reaches 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], a size that is among the largest recorded for the Lutjanus genus in the Indo-Pacific region. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight derived from this asymptotic length is approximately 7,900 grams [Wwi = approximately 7,900 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required to achieve such dimensions in a demersal predatory fish. Individuals of this size are typically apex predators within their reef habitat, feeding on a diet dominated by crustaceans, cephalopods, and small teleosts. Growth rates slow considerably after the onset of sexual maturity as resources are increasingly directed toward gamete production rather than continued body growth. Tag-recapture studies indicate that the von Bertalanffy growth coefficient is relatively low, consistent with a long-lived, slow-growing life history adapted to stable tropical reef environments.

Reproductive output is substantial, with females releasing multiple batches of pelagic eggs over the extended spawning season. The maximum lifespan documented in wild populations reaches 20 years [am = 20 years] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a longevity that is typical for large lutjanid species inhabiting relatively stable tropical reef systems where natural mortality rates are low. Age determination using otolith microincrement analysis confirms that individuals can persist for two decades under natural conditions, with the oldest recorded specimen exhibiting 20 annual growth zones. This extended lifespan allows for repeated reproductive events across many seasons, a classic iteroparous strategy that buffers against years of poor recruitment. Comparative studies with other lutjanids indicate that lifetime reproductive output scales positively with body size and longevity.

Comparative physiological studies have examined the thermal sensitivity of reproductive processes in Lutjanus malabaricus, given that spawning activity is tightly coupled to seasonal temperature cycles. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the gonadosomatic index peaked at 20% [GSI = 20%]. Females become reproductively mature once they surpass a fork length of 57.6 centimeters [Lp = 57.6 centimeters], a threshold that integrates both somatic growth and environmental conditions. The asymptotic body size of this species, as reflected by an ultimate fork length of 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], is rarely attained due to the combined pressures of fishing mortality and natural senescence. The maximum recorded longevity of 20 years [am = 20 years] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] places this species among the longer-lived members of its family, with otolith-derived ages confirming that post-reproductive individuals are occasionally observed in unfished populations. This suite of life-history traits positions Lutjanus malabaricus as a species with moderate resilience to exploitation, though its vulnerability to overfishing is notable given the extended time required to reach sexual maturity and the slow replacement rate inherent to long-lived fishes.
